=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of Seller Package

**Bottom line:** The Seller's package is not acceptable as a basis for mark-up. It asks the Buyer to accept a framework that removes most of the protection a warranty-and-indemnity SPA is meant to provide, and it supports that with unverified "market" assertions and a "[STANDARD]/FINAL" labelling scheme. I have not limited the review to [OPEN] items. Every item below is treated as open.

**Limits of this review:** I am working from the Seller's summaries and disclosure letter, not the underlying data room documents (DD-001 to DD-012). Several points below depend on those documents, and the NSW-specific points (non-reliance enforceability, privacy obligations, payroll tax, superannuation) should be confirmed by NSW counsel and the Buyer's tax and privacy advisers.

---

## A. Process and framing

**1. The "[STANDARD]" and "FINAL" labels do not bind the Buyer.** The Seller says these positions were settled "at principal level" and are "not intended to be re-opened," and asks the reviewer to skip [STANDARD] items. Nothing in the package shows the Buyer agreed to any of these terms. The deal team should confirm whether any written, signed principal-level agreement exists. If none does, the Buyer should say so expressly in the mark-up cover note and reserve all rights.

**2. The "market context" is advocacy, not evidence.** The 10–20% cap, ~1% basket, 12–18 month limitation and buyer-knowledge qualification are presented as "widely accepted." The Buyer should test these against its own precedent set or a W&I/M&A adviser's data before accepting them as a benchmark. Even if they were typical, the specific risks in this deal (Section C) justify departing from them.

---

## B. General warranty package (Seller's Clauses 8.3, 9.3, 12, 13, 20.5)

**3. Buyer-knowledge bar (Clause 8.3): reject.** The clause bars claims for any matter the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records. Combined with the general disclosure in Section 4 below, this would bar claims on nearly everything the Buyer diligenced, which is the purpose of diligence. Under NSW law, Buyers generally retain warranty claims despite their knowledge unless the contract says otherwise, so this clause would be a significant change. **Pushback:** delete 8.3 entirely. If the Seller insists on something, limit it to matters *fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter against the specific warranty*.

**4. Data room and register disclosure (Disclosure Letter 1.1, 1.2; Schedule 7): reject.** The Seller discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room and public registers. That is a blanket disclosure of everything, which would defeat the warranties. Disclosure should only qualify a specific warranty, be fairly disclosed (so that a reasonable reader can identify the matter), and be made against that warranty. **Pushback:** strike 1.1 and 1.2. Require specific, fairly disclosed disclosures only, with a clear statement that general data room access is not disclosure.

**5. General cap at 20% of price (AUD 4.8m) (Clause 12.1).** Given the known exposures in Section C, a 20% cap is too low. **Pushback:** raise the general cap substantially (the Buyer should set this figure with its advisers, but it should be well above AUD 4.8m) and exclude from it fundamental warranties, tax, and specific indemnities.

**6. Thresholds (Clause 12.2): de minimis AUD 25,000 and true deductible basket AUD 250,000.** The basket is about 1.04% of price, and as drafted only the excess over it is recoverable, so the Buyer absorbs the first AUD 250,000 of losses. The de minimis would also exclude individual claims below AUD 25,000, which could include some privacy-related or contract-related losses. **Pushback:** convert the basket to a tipping basket (once exceeded, recovery from the first dollar), reduce the basket (the Buyer should set a figure, but a lower percentage is the starting point), and reduce the de minimis, or aggregate related claims so that a series of small claims arising from the same facts counts toward the basket.

**7. Time limits (Clauses 12.3 / 13): 18 months, and the sweep-up provision.** Eighteen months is short for matters that may surface later, including privacy regulator action, supplier disputes, IP ownership challenges, and tax assessments. The Seller also proposes that any limitation "applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise," which would pull title, capacity, and tax claims into the 18-month regime. **Pushback:** general warranties of 24–36 months; fundamental warranties and title for 6 years or the statutory period, whichever is longer; tax claims until 60 days after the relevant assessment period closes. Reject the sweep-up provision.

**8. Fundamental and title warranties (Seller's "administrative simplicity" proposal): reject.** Title and capacity warranties go to whether the Buyer actually gets what it is paying for. They should not share the general cap or time limits. **Pushback:** title and capacity capped at the purchase price (AUD 24m) and surviving for at least 6 years, or the statutory period if longer.

**9. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance (Clauses 9.3, 12.8, 20.5): reject as drafted.** The Seller applies these to "all Claims of any nature." At a minimum, the Buyer should carve out fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, and specific indemnities. The non-reliance clause should not exclude fraud, and the Buyer should check with NSW counsel how a non-reliance clause interacts with misleading or deceptive conduct claims under the Australian Consumer Law (noting that the position for a commercial share sale may differ from a consumer transaction). **Pushback:** carve-outs for fraud and the categories above; exclusive remedy language limited to general warranty claims only.

---

## C. Known issues and their risk allocation

**10. Bluefen change-of-control consent (Clause 3 / 6.3; Disclosure §2).** Bluefen accounts for about AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%). The Seller's own disclosure confirms the consent has not been delivered and the conditions in clause 11.3 are not evidenced as satisfied. The Seller's proposal is "reasonable endeavours" and treating consent as satisfied on delivery of written consent. This would move the risk of losing 30% of revenue to the Buyer after Completion, and the "addressed" language overstates the position. **Pushback:** make written Bluefen consent, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer, with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived in writing, a condition precedent to Completion, with a termination right if not received by a long-stop date. If the Buyer is prepared to proceed without it, require a price adjustment or escrow and a specific indemnity for loss of revenue attributable to Bluefen termination or repricing.

**11. Riverlark facility (Clauses 2 / 7; Disclosure §3).** About AUD 3.2m is outstanding, unpaid, with security not yet discharged. The Seller proposes a release "following Completion." That is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal, where the debt should be deducted from the price and repaid at Completion. **Pushback:** the Riverlark payout should be paid from the funds flow at Completion, with a payout letter and an executed discharge of security (and PPSR release) delivered at Completion, held in escrow if necessary. The Buyer should run its own PPSR search to confirm there is no other security over the Company's assets.

**12. Ironquay IP (Clause 11.1; DD-004 clause 7.3; DD-010; Disclosure §4).** Under DD-004, the transfer of SOW3 project materials is conditional on payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 as open, and there is no evidence of payment or of a confirmatory assignment in the data room. The Seller's indemnity is limited to the SOW3 payment and described as "adequate." It is not adequate. If the Company does not validly own the materials, that goes to title over key IP. **Pushback:** (a) pay the AUD 180,000 before Completion, or treat it as a debt-like deduction from price; (b) require an executed confirmatory assignment of all Ironquay project materials as a condition precedent; (c) a specific indemnity covering all Ironquay ownership, third-party and related claims, not limited to the SOW3 payment, outside the basket and general cap, with survival matching the fundamental warranties.

**13. Employee Completion bonuses (DD-005; Disclosure §5).** The AUD 420,000 in conditional bonuses is not in the draft funds flow, and the disclosure does not say whether payroll tax or superannuation applies. In a debt-free/cash-free deal these are debt-like items. Payroll tax under NSW rules may apply to some or all of the bonuses (the current general rate should be confirmed with the Buyer's tax adviser), and superannuation guarantee at 12% may also be payable depending on how the bonuses are classified. Indicatively, the on-costs could add tens of thousands of dollars on top of the AUD 420,000. **Pushback:** treat the bonuses and all related on-costs as debt-like items deducted from the price, or have the Seller bear them as a transaction cost. Require a full employee schedule showing amounts, conditions, and on-costs, and warranties on accrued entitlements.

**14. Export and privacy incident (DD-006; Disclosure §6; Seller's 4.6 / Schedule 6).** The Seller calls this "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." The facts are: a download link for a file of about 1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) was sent to an unintended external address; no determination has been made as to whether anyone accessed it, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. If the Company is an APP entity and this is an eligible data breach, there are assessment and notification timing obligations under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) that may already be running (the 30-day assessment period is relevant, measured from when the Company became aware of the issue). The date of discovery is not in the package and should be requested.
**Pushback:** require (a) the date the Company became aware of the incident, (b) the forensic findings and current status of the eligible data breach assessment, (c) confirmation of any notifications, (d) a specific indemnity for all losses arising from the incident (regulatory investigation and penalties to the extent insurable or lawful to indemnify, notification costs, remediation, third-party claims), outside the basket and general cap, surviving at least 3 years, and (e) a dedicated escrow or retention if the assessment is not complete before signing.

**15. Office lease (DD-007; Disclosure §7).** DD-007 identifies a notification obligation but does not say whether landlord consent is needed for the share sale. **Pushback:** obtain a landlord confirmation or consent (or a landlord estoppel) that the sale does not breach the lease, as a condition precedent or a specific warranty backed by indemnity.

**16. Three Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate; DD-008 and DD-011; Disclosure §8).** The Seller calls these ordinary-course costs. The disclosure says it cannot be determined whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course. The disclosure also says they should be read together for timing and scope, which suggests they may have been split across documents. **Pushback:** require the three contracts, their terms (including termination rights and any change-of-control provisions), and the timing. Any commitment beyond Completion should be subject to Buyer consent under the interim conduct covenants, and any accrued or committed amount should be treated as debt-like. Ask whether the three renewals were negotiated as one arrangement.

**17. Mossvale assignment restriction (DD-009; Disclosure §9).** The Seller's disclosure does not say the sale triggers the restriction. **Pushback:** obtain written confirmation from Mossvale (or a reasoned legal opinion) that no consent is required for the share sale, or a specific warranty backed by indemnity.

**18. Title to shares (DD-012; Disclosure §10).** The only evidence the Seller offers is the share register that the Seller itself holds. The disclosure says the Buyer has not verified title. **Pushback:** require an ASIC company extract, copies of share certificates, the executed transfer documents, and a statutory register inspection before signing. Require a title warranty that the Seller is the sole legal and beneficial owner, free from encumbrances, with a release of any security over the shares. This is a fundamental warranty (see item 8).

---

## D. Summary of recommendations

**Reject outright:**
- The "[STANDARD]/FINAL" framing and the instruction to skip cleared items. Reserve all rights in the mark-up.
- The buyer-knowledge bar (8.3).
- Blanket data room and register disclosure (1.1, 1.2, Schedule 7).
- Extending the general cap, time limits, and limitations to title, capacity, and tax.
- The "adequate" characterisation of the Ironquay indemnity.
- The "reasonable endeavours" treatment of Bluefen consent.

**Require before signing or Completion:**
1. Written Bluefen consent with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived (condition precedent, or price adjustment and escrow if waived).
2. Riverlark payout and security discharge delivered at Completion from the funds flow.
3. Ironquay AUD 180,000 paid (or deducted from price), plus a confirmatory assignment of all project materials.
4. Bonuses (AUD 420,000) and on-costs treated as debt-like items, reflected in the funds flow.
5. Privacy incident: discovery date, assessment status, and notification position, plus a specific indemnity and escrow.
6. Landlord confirmation (lease) and Mossvale confirmation (no consent needed).
7. Sandbar contracts reviewed, renewals subject to consent, and accrued amounts treated as debt-like.
8. Independent verification of title (ASIC extract, share certificates, transfer documents, register inspection).

**Counter-proposals to table:**
- General cap raised substantially above AUD 4.8m (figure to be set with advisers).
- Tipping basket with a lower threshold and a lower de minimis, or aggregation of related claims.
- General survival 24–36 months.
- Fundamental and title warranties capped at price, surviving 6 years or the statutory period.
- Tax claims survive until 60 days after the limitation period.
- Specific indemnities (Bluefen, Ironquay, privacy incident, leases and supplier contracts where relevant), outside the basket and general cap.
- Carve-outs from limitations and non-reliance for fraud.

**Quantified exposure (indicative, from the Seller's own figures):** Riverlark AUD 3.2m, Ironquay AUD 180k, bonuses AUD 420k, and Sandbar AUD 330k come to about AUD 4.13m before on-costs and before any Bluefen revenue risk (AUD 3.6m annual revenue) or the unquantified privacy exposure. Several of these are debt-like and should reduce the price under a debt-free/cash-free mechanism rather than sit with the Buyer as warranty risk.

**Next steps:** Verify each point against the underlying data room documents; have NSW counsel confirm the non-reliance, Australian Consumer Law, and Privacy Act positions; have the tax adviser confirm payroll tax and superannuation on the bonuses; and prepare a full mark-up with the reservation of rights above.

Office lease (DD-007; Disclosure §7).** DD-007 identifies a notification obligation but does not say whether landlord consent is needed for the share sale. **Pushback:** obtain a landlord confirmation or consent (or a landlord estoppel) that the sale does not breach the lease, as a condition precedent or a specific warranty backed by indemnity.

**16. Three Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate; DD-008 and DD-011; Disclosure §8).** The Seller calls these ordinary-course costs. The disclosure says it cannot be determined whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course. The disclosure also says they should be read together for timing and scope, which suggests they may have been split across documents. **Pushback:** require the three contracts, their terms (including termination rights and any change-of-control provisions), and the timing. Any commitment beyond Completion should be subject to Buyer consent under the interim conduct covenants, and any accrued or committed amount should be treated as debt-like. Ask whether the three renewals were negotiated as one arrangement.

**17. Mossvale assignment restriction (DD-009; Disclosure §9).** The Seller's disclosure does not say the sale triggers the restriction. **Pushback:** obtain written confirmation from Mossvale (or a reasoned legal opinion) that no consent is required for the share sale, or a specific warranty backed by indemnity.

**18. Title to shares (DD-012; Disclosure §10).** The only evidence the Seller offers is the share register that the Seller itself holds. The disclosure says the Buyer has not verified title. **Pushback:** require an ASIC company extract, copies of share certificates, the executed transfer documents, and a statutory register inspection before signing. Require a title warranty that the Seller is the sole legal and beneficial owner, free from encumbrances, with a release of any security over the shares. This is a fundamental warranty (see item 8).

## D. Summary of recommendations

**Reject outright:**
- The "[STANDARD]/FINAL" framing and the instruction to skip cleared items. Reserve all rights in the mark-up.
- The buyer-knowledge bar (8.3).
- Blanket data room and register disclosure (1.1, 1.2, Schedule 7).
- Extending the general cap, time limits, and limitations to title, capacity, and tax.
- The "adequate" characterisation of the Ironquay indemnity.
- The "reasonable endeavours" treatment of Bluefen consent.

**Require before signing or Completion:**
1. Written Bluefen consent with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived (condition precedent, or price adjustment and escrow if waived).
2. Riverlark payout and security discharge delivered at Completion from the funds flow.
3. Ironquay AUD 180,000 paid (or deducted from price), plus a confirmatory assignment of all project materials.
4. Bonuses (AUD 420,000) and on-costs treated as debt-like items, reflected in the funds flow.
5. Privacy incident: discovery date, assessment status, and notification position, plus a specific indemnity and escrow.
6. Landlord confirmation (lease) and Mossvale confirmation (no consent needed).
7. Sandbar contracts reviewed, renewals subject to consent, and accrued amounts treated as debt-like.
8. Independent verification of title (ASIC extract, share certificates, transfer documents, register inspection).

**Counter-proposals to table:**
- General cap raised substantially above AUD 4.8m (figure to be set with advisers).
- Tipping basket with a lower threshold and a lower de minimis, or aggregation of related claims.
- General survival 24–36 months.
- Fundamental and title warranties capped at price, surviving 6 years or the statutory period.
- Tax claims survive until 60 days after the limitation period.
- Specific indemnities (Bluefen, Ironquay, privacy incident, leases and supplier contracts where relevant), outside the basket and general cap.
- Carve-outs from limitations and non-reliance for fraud.

**Quantified exposure (indicative, from the Seller's own figures):** Riverlark AUD 3.2m, Ironquay AUD 180k, bonuses AUD 420k, and Sandbar AUD 330k come to about AUD 4.13m before on-costs and before any Bluefen revenue risk (AUD 3.6m annual revenue) or the unquantified privacy exposure. Several of these are debt-like and should reduce the price under a debt-free/cash-free mechanism rather than sit with the Buyer as warranty risk.

**Next steps:** Verify each point against the underlying data room documents; have NSW counsel confirm the non-reliance, Australian Consumer Law, and Privacy Act positions; have the tax adviser confirm payroll tax and superannuation on the bonuses; and prepare a full mark-up with the reservation of rights above.
